The Blackbar devil (Plectroglyphidodon dickii) is a damselfish species commonly associated with coral reefs across the Indo-Pacific region. Field studies have documented that newly emerged yolk-sac larvae, following eclosion, possess a wet weight at birth of just 0.00032 grams [Wwb = 0.00032 grams], a remarkably small mass that reflects the tiny diameter of the fertilised eggs. The embryonic development leading to this hatching event proceeds at a water temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], under which conditions the age at birth from the point of fertilisation is approximately 5.3 days [ab = approximately 5.3 days]. This rapid progression from syngamy to larval eclosion is typical of many tropical pomacentrids, where elevated thermal regimes accelerate embryogenesis. The initial body mass is consistent with values reported for the congeneric species Chromis chromis, from which the egg diameter data were originally derived, and underscores the high fecundity necessary to offset substantial larval mortality in the planktonic environment.

As juveniles grow and approach the transition to the adult stage, their standard length increases steadily until they attain the size at which gonadal maturation begins. Puberty in this species is initiated once individuals reach a standard length of 5 centimeters [Lp = 5 centimeters], a developmental milestone that marks the onset of gametogenesis and the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. At this same life stage, the wet weight at puberty has been estimated at approximately 2.4 grams [Wwp = approximately 2.4 grams], a body mass that represents a considerable increase from the minuscule mass recorded at hatching. This weight value was derived from a length-weight relationship commonly applied to damselfishes, where ultimate standard length is a key predictor of mass. The attainment of this size and mass typically occurs within the first year of benthic life, after which individuals begin to establish and defend feeding territories on the reef substrate, transitioning from a pelagic larval existence to a more sedentary, site-attached adult lifestyle.

Reproductive activity in sexually mature Blackbar devil individuals is strongly influenced by local water temperature, and field observations have been conducted under stable thermal conditions. At a sustained water temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], the daily reproductive rate is remarkably high, with females capable of producing approximately 200 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 200 eggs per day]. This elevated output is comparable to the maximum spawning rates reported for the closely related species Chromis chromis, upon which these estimates are based, and reflects an iteroparous strategy typical of small-bodied reef fishes that invest heavily in continuous, high-frequency gamete production. The reproductive season may extend over several months in tropical waters, allowing females to release many thousands of eggs across a single breeding period, with each spawning event contributing to the total daily fecundity that sustains local population dynamics on the reef.

The ultimate body size that an adult Blackbar devil can achieve is constrained by both genetic factors and the ecological conditions of its habitat. Long-term field surveys have recorded a maximum standard length of 11.6 centimeters [Li = 11.6 centimeters] for the largest individuals, a value that defines the upper boundary of somatic growth for this species. The corresponding ultimate wet weight, calculated from the length-mass allometry typical of pomacentrids, is approximately 29.65 grams [Wwi = approximately 29.65 grams], indicating a relatively modest adult body size compared to larger damselfish congeners. This asymptotic mass is attained after several years of growth, during which the fish shift from a diet of planktonic copepods to one dominated by benthic algae and small invertebrates. The relationship between length and mass in this species follows the same general pattern observed across many coral-reef teleosts, where body condition reflects both resource availability and the energetic demands of territory defence.

Longevity records for Plectroglyphidodon dickii indicate that the species possesses a moderate lifespan relative to other small-bodied coral-reef fishes. The maximum recorded longevity under natural conditions in the wild is 4,380 days [am = 4,380 days], which corresponds to approximately 12 years, when the fish are maintained at the typical reef temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C]. This considerable lifespan allows for multiple reproductive seasons and a protracted period of territory ownership, both of which are advantageous in the competitive reef environment where suitable shelter sites are limited. Senescence in this species is thought to be gradual, with older individuals exhibiting reduced mobility and a decline in condition factor before eventual natural mortality. This extended life history, combined with high daily fecundity and relatively late maturation, positions the Blackbar devil as an equilibrium-oriented strategist well adapted to stable coral-reef habitats.
